title: Ang 12–13: Sohila
hook: the night hymns close the opening; the daily prayers are the Granth's gateway
tomorrow: what if you were handed a palace made of pearls?

segments.voice: Yesterday, So Purakh: the evening pages, where the Gurus after Guru Nanak still sign as Nanak, and the heading tells you who's speaking. Now, the night.

A playlist sorted neatly by genre, except someone has pinned a handful of mixed songs to the very top. That's the odd thing about the Granth's first pages. The book is arranged by raga, the musical moods, and the raga order opens with Sri Rag. But Sri Rag doesn't start until ang fourteen. Before it, the headings jump around: Asa, Gujri, Gauri, Dhanasri. Why would a book ordered by raga open with a mix?
screen: `A PLAYLIST WITH A MIX PINNED ON TOP.` → `SRI RAG WAITS UNTIL ANG 14.` → `WHY OPEN WITH A MIX?`

segments.voice: Look at what's pinned. The Japji, said in the morning. So Dar and So Purakh, the Rehras, said in the evening. And on angs twelve and thirteen, the Sohila, said at night before sleep. Each Sohila hymn sits under its own raga heading, and the set closes the opening pages. So the mix isn't a mess. It's the daily round: morning, evening and night, placed in front of everything else. Some readers call these pages the Granth's gateway: you pass through the prayers you say every day before the ragas begin. Something to tell someone tonight: a reader who knows only the daily prayers already knows the Granth's first thirteen pages. And the night prayer has a picture worth carrying to bed. In one hymn, under Dhanasri, Guru Nanak describes an aarti, the waving of lamps, with no tray at all. In the original: gagan mai thaal rav chand deepak bane. The sky is the platter, the sun and the moon are the lamps. The gateway closes on the whole night sky.
screen: `MORNING, EVENING, NIGHT: PINNED FIRST.` · `SOHILA: THE NIGHT PRAYER.` · `THE DAILY ROUND BEFORE THE RAGAS.` · `THE SKY IS THE PLATTER.` · then, large: `THE GATEWAY.`

segments.voice: If it's dark where you are, look out a window at the sky for a while, whatever lights it: a moon, a star, a streetlamp. If it's daytime, rest your eyes on one light near you instead. Let it be the lamp on the platter, and breathe slowly while you look.
Ang 12. Where the Sohila, the night prayer, begins and closes the Granth's opening pages. Today's word.
Your line: the gateway. Morning, evening and night first, and only then the ragas. Good night.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape puzzle. The odd detail (a book ordered by raga that opens with mixed raga headings) is solved by the daily round: the morning, evening and night prayers placed first, a gateway before Sri Rag.
'Some readers call these pages the Granth's gateway' is hedged; the outline uses the word. Confirm.

The Sohila's hymns: Gauri Deepaki M1, Asa M1, Dhanasri M1, Gauri Purbi M4, Gauri Purbi M5 (not counted aloud). The hook lists headings seen before Ang 14 (Asa, Gujri, Gauri, Dhanasri); confirm Gujri appears in the Rehras hymns on Ang 10.
'The first thirteen pages' rests on the Ang numbers of the standard 1430-ang saroop. Confirm.
Quoted original 'gagan mai thaal rav chand deepak bane' (Ang 13). The aarti hymn was taught in depth in years 2 and 4 (days 427–428, 1085); here it is one image.
Practice rotation: look at one object (a light, or the sky).
